drills.q: What is the size-balance invariant that two heaps must maintain, and why does it matter?
drills.a: The two heap sizes must never differ by more than 1. This is what guarantees the median is always exactly at one or both heap tops, giving O(1) median access instead of requiring a deeper traversal.

drills.q: When the two heaps are equal in size, how do you compute the median? When one has exactly one more element, how do you compute it?
drills.a: Equal sizes: average the max-heap's top and the min-heap's top. One extra element (always in the max-heap/small half, by the invariant): the median is simply that heap's top alone, no averaging.

drills.q: Derive why two-heap insertion is O(log n) while inserting into a maintained-sorted array is O(n), even though both use a comparison that could be found via binary search in O(log n).
drills.a: Binary search locates the correct position in O(log n) in both cases. The difference is what happens AFTER locating the position: a heap only needs to sift the new element up or down through at most log2(n) levels to restore the heap property, touching O(log n) elements total. A sorted array must physically shift every element after the insertion point over by one slot to make room, which touches up to O(n) elements in the worst case (inserting near the front). The heap's relaxed ordering (only parent-child order, not full sequential order) is what avoids the shifting cost.

drills.q: A candidate implements the running-median insert by comparing the new value only against the current median and pushing directly into what seems like the 'obviously correct' heap, skipping the cross-heap push-and-pop step. Construct a sequence of insertions where this produces a wrong median, and explain the fix.
drills.a: Consider inserting 1, 2, 3, 4 in that order with a naive 'compare to current median, push directly' approach that never cross-validates: after 1, 2 median-ish comparisons can leave both heaps technically valid-looking but with an element in the 'wrong' heap relative to its true rank once more elements arrive (e.g., 3 pushed to the large heap based on being greater than a stale median, when it should end up as the new boundary element). The robust algorithm avoids ambiguity entirely by always pushing every new value into ONE designated heap first (say, small), then unconditionally popping that heap's current top and pushing it into the other heap, then checking sizes and moving one element back if needed. This three-step discipline guarantees the ordering invariant holds regardless of where the new value 'should' end up, because the cross-push step re-sorts across both heaps using their own top comparisons rather than trusting the caller's guess.

drills.q: Design the lazy-deletion mechanism needed for Sliding Window Median, and explain exactly when a pending removal is actually applied.
drills.a: Maintain a hash map from value to a count of how many pending removals are outstanding for that value. When the sliding window moves and an element falls out, increment its pending-removal count instead of touching the heap immediately. Whenever you're about to trust a heap's top as the current true extreme (during a median query, or during a rebalance/cross-push step), first check whether that top value has a positive pending-removal count; if so, pop it, decrement its count, and repeat the check on the new top, before using it. This defers the O(n)-scan cost of true removal until the stale value would have surfaced anyway, turning it into an O(log n) pop at that point.

drills.q: A monitoring team wants to track p99 latency incrementally across a single process using the two-heap technique, then later merge results from 200 separate processes into one fleet-wide p99. What works for the single-process case, and what breaks for the fleet-wide merge?
drills.a: For a single process, the generalized two-heap technique works well: keep the heap-size ratio at roughly 99:1 instead of 50:50, and the boundary value between the two heaps is the running p99 latency, updated in O(log n) per new data point. For the fleet-wide merge across 200 processes, this breaks down: two independent two-heap structures (each built from a different process's local stream) don't have a simple, correct way to be combined into one structure representing the true combined p99 -- you can't just merge heaps arbitrarily and expect the balance invariant and ordering guarantee to still hold relative to the full combined dataset. This is precisely the gap that approximate, explicitly mergeable sketches like t-digest or DDSketch are designed to fill: they support a defined merge operation across independently-built sketches while preserving bounded error on the resulting combined percentile estimate.

drills.q: Explain why Median of Two Sorted Arrays (LC4) is not solved with two heaps, and what the efficient approach is instead.
drills.a: Both input arrays are already fully sorted and are static (not a stream with ongoing insertions), so there's no incremental-update problem to justify building and maintaining a heap-based structure at all -- doing so would cost O(m+n) to construct the heaps for a single one-shot computation. The efficient approach is a binary search over the partition point of the shorter array (checking m+n total elements split into a 'left half' and 'right half' such that every left-half element is <= every right-half element across both arrays), achieving O(log(min(m,n))), which beats even reading through both arrays once.

drills.q: Distinguish the data structure and complexity used for 'Kth Largest Element in a Stream' from the two-heap running-median structure, and explain why conflating them is a common mistake.
drills.a: Kth Largest Element in a Stream uses a single min-heap capped at size k: if a new value is greater than the heap's current minimum once the heap is full, pop the minimum and push the new value; the heap's top is always the k-th largest value seen so far. This is O(log k) per insertion and O(k) space. The running-median structure instead uses TWO heaps holding ALL elements seen so far (not just the top k), split into balanced halves, to expose the middle value. The conflation is common because both involve heaps and streaming data, but they answer structurally different questions: 'what are the top k' (bounded retention, discard everything else) versus 'what's the value in the middle of everything' (must retain every element, split into two balanced groups).
